beginner: The Federal Reserve stopped cutting interest rates in April after three meetings of holding steady, but four officials voted to start raising rates again, the most dissent in over 30 years. War with Iran drove oil and gas prices up sharply, pushing inflation back to 3.3% in March, the highest in nearly two years.

The Fed faces a genuine split: inflation is climbing again due to energy shocks, yet the economy is not overheating. The four dissenting votes signal real concern that holding rates at 3.5% is too loose given the price surge, even though unemployment sits at a reasonable 4.4%.

Watch whether the April inflation print softens the hawkish pressure or whether the Fed eventually caves to the dissenters and raises rates. A sustained inflation above 2.3% would force the central bank's hand by mid-year.
moderate: CPI jumped to 3.3% in March, driven almost entirely by oil and gas prices spiking to four-year highs after the Iran conflict erupted. The Fed held rates at 3.5%, but four officials dissented in favor of tightening, the first time since October 1992 that so many broke ranks.

This mirrors the energy shock of 2022, except unemployment is lower and wage growth is more contained. The dissent matters because it telegraphs serious concern about secondary inflation spreading if oil stays elevated, even though the core consumer is not yet panicking.
The forecast assumes inflation will ease to 2.3% by year-end, which requires oil prices to normalize quickly. If they don't, expect rate hike votes to intensify in coming meetings.
expert: CPI 3.3% YoY in March 2026 (February was 2.41%) reflects energy shocks dominating the print. The 8-4 dissent in April, the first significant hawkish split since late 1992, signals Fed officials believe terminal rates have moved higher in the rate reaction function due to geopolitical risk premium in energy markets.

Unemployment 4.4% (February) and core inflation dynamics remain benign, but the dissent is not about current slack, it is about tail risk of anchoring slippage if elevated energy persists. The four dissenters likely see a higher equilibrium real rate needed in a higher-oil-price regime.

Forward watch: May CPI print and the next FOMC meeting. If headline CPI stays above 3% while core remains tame, expect 50-75 bps of rate hike votes to accumulate by Q3, forcing a June or July decision point despite the forecast's 2.3% year-end assumption.

beginner: Canada's government cut the gas tax by 10 cents per liter for five months starting April, a direct bid to ease household fuel costs and inflation pressures. Unemployment fell from 7.1% in September to 6.7% in March, showing the labor market is tightening after a rough winter.

The tax cut is a political response to energy shocks hitting consumers hard, but it will also mask real inflation in April and May CPI readings. A strengthening job market means the Bank of Canada can stay patient on rate cuts, even though inflation was only 1.78% in February.

The central bank cut rates to 2.25% and will watch whether the fuel tax suspension causes inflation expectations to drift, which could force it to hold steady longer than the 1.7% growth forecast might otherwise allow.
moderate: The federal fuel excise tax suspension runs April 20 through September 7, shaving roughly 10 cents per liter off gas prices and directly cutting inflation prints for those months. This is unusual fiscal intervention into price levels, signaling the government sees household energy squeeze as a political and economic problem.

Unemployment fell 40 bps from September's peak of 7.1% to 6.7%, a meaningful tightening that contradicts the 1.1% real GDP growth forecast for 2026. The job market strength suggests slack is smaller than consensus expects, which may keep the Bank of Canada from cutting as aggressively as peers.

The fuel tax holiday will artificially depress April and May CPI, masking underlying inflation trends. When the cut expires in September, inflation prints will spike mechanically, creating a false impression of re-acceleration and complicating monetary policy signaling in the second half.
expert: The fuel excise tax suspension (April 20 to September 7, 2026) is a direct fiscal supply shock that will reduce headline CPI by approximately 40-50 bps in Q2 and early Q3, then reverse sharply in Q4. February CPI was 1.78%, well below the 2% year-end forecast, suggesting underlying inflation is already soft.

Unemployment fell to 6.7% in March from 7.1% in September 2025, contradicting the 6.5% year-end forecast and implying tighter labour slack than consensus. The policy rate at 2.25% in February will likely stay flat through mid-year, despite growth underperforming at 1.1% versus the 1.7% full-year expectation.

Watch the July and August CPI prints for underlying momentum before the tax cut expires. If core CPI remains below 2% even after fuel normalization, the BoC will have room for cuts in Q4, but if it pops above 2.3% post-expiry, the central bank may signal a hold into 2027.

beginner: The UK economy is slowing because of the Middle East war pushing up energy costs and the Bank of England cutting rates more slowly than the US Federal Reserve. Growth is now projected to slide below 1.3%, a material miss from earlier expectations.

Higher energy prices are putting pressure on UK consumers and businesses at a time when the central bank wants to move cautiously on rate cuts. This leaves the UK in a tougher spot than most peers: high energy costs and limited monetary relief.

Watch whether inflation stays above 2.5% or falls sharply. If energy prices stay elevated and growth disappoints further, the Bank of England may be forced to cut rates despite inflation concerns, creating a policy dilemma.
moderate: The UK faces a geopolitical energy shock that is dampening growth (now below 1.3%) while the Bank of England moves slower on rate cuts than the Fed or ECB. February CPI was 3.24%, well above the 2.5% year-end forecast, and the policy rate at 3.75% means limited near-term cuts.

The growth slowdown reflects both external energy shocks and the lagged impact of earlier rate hikes that the central bank now wants to reverse. But elevated energy-driven inflation constrains how fast the BoE can ease, creating a scissors dynamic: growth pressure argues for cuts, inflation argues against them.

The 2.5% full-year inflation forecast assumes energy prices normalize. If they don't, UK inflation will stay sticky above 3% and the BoE will need to defend its credibility by holding rates higher for longer, accepting slower growth as the cost of anchor stability.
expert: Growth projection downgrade to below 1.3% (from prior 1.5-1.8% expectations) is driven by elevated energy costs reducing real incomes and business capex, while the slower BoE easing cycle relative to the Fed creates a real rate headwind. February CPI 3.24% remains above the 2.5% year-end forecast, implying modest disinflation path from here.

The BoE policy rate at 3.75% in February (same as the Fed's 3.5-3.75%) masks a tighter real rate environment in the UK due to higher headline inflation and energy expectations. The central bank faces a negative supply shock (energy) that typically argues for maintaining nominal rates but accepting lower growth, rather than cutting into the shock.

Key indicator: the August CPI print for Q3 momentum. If energy prices roll over and CPI falls to 2.3% or below, the BoE will have cover for 75-100 bps of cuts in H2 2026. If energy remains elevated and CPI stays above 2.7%, expect the BoE to cut only 25-50 bps total, leaving UK real rates restrictive and growth forecast at risk of a downside revision below 1%.

beginner: Japan's economy is slowing sharply to 0.4% growth for 2026, down from 1.1% expected for 2025, because US tariffs are hitting Japanese exporters hard. The central bank raised rates to 0.75% and signaled further tightening, betting that the economy can handle higher borrowing costs after 30 years of deflation.

For the first time in nearly a decade, Japan's economy is running so hot (excess demand in Q2 2025) that the Bank of Japan believes it can raise rates without triggering recession. This is a historic shift from the deflation-fighting era that dominated the past three decades.

Watch US trade policy closely. If tariffs intensify and growth falls further, the BoJ may have to pause rate hikes despite inflation finally taking hold. The tariff shock is the key variable determining whether Japan's inflation cycle survives.
moderate: The 2026 growth forecast collapsed to 0.4% from 1.1% expected for 2025, entirely due to anticipated US tariff impacts on Japanese manufacturing and exports. The BoJ raised rates to 0.75% in February and signaled more hikes coming, betting it can normalize policy without triggering deflation relapse.

Japan reported 0.3% excess demand in Q2 2025, the first positive output gap since 2019. This gives the BoJ political cover to raise rates despite CPI being only 1.26%, because officials believe the output gap will persist even as tariffs bite. The calculation assumes tariff damage will shrink activity but not eliminate slack creation.

The tariff scenario is critical. If US-Japan trade tensions ease and growth stabilizes above 1%, the BoJ will continue tightening toward 1.5-2% by year-end. If tariffs deepen and growth slips toward 0%, the BoJ will face a credibility test: does it pause hikes to support growth, or push through to anchor a freshly-emerged inflation cycle?
expert: 2026 growth forecast collapse from 1.1% to 0.4% YoY is a 70 bp downside revision driven by incremental US tariff implementation materializing across H2 2025 and H1 2026. The BoJ raised the policy rate to 0.75% in February and signaled further tightening despite CPI only 1.26%, betting on a stable positive output gap (0.3% in Q2 2025) that can absorb multiple rate hikes.

The excess-demand status in Q2 2025 (first time since early 2019) is the BoJ's primary justification for hiking into a growth slowdown, but this assumes the output gap does not reverse faster than the tariff deceleration. February CPI 1.26% is barely above the 1.8% year-end forecast, leaving little room for secondary inflation if tariffs surprise on the upside or if wage momentum accelerates.

Inflection point: Q3 2026 growth prints and US tariff announcements. If growth undershoots 0.4% while the output gap inverts negative, the BoJ will be forced to pause hikes and potentially signal a cut in Q4, reversing the normalization narrative. If growth stabilizes and tariff uncertainty eases, expect 25-50 bps more in hikes through Q4, targeting 1.25-1.5% by year-end.

beginner: Germany's economy is being squeezed by geopolitical shocks that push up energy costs while its trading partners stay sluggish, making domestic spending the only real engine right now.
Inflation at 1.9% in February sits comfortably below the European Central Bank's 2% target, giving policymakers room to hold steady rather than tighten further.
The unemployment rate stuck at 3.6% shows the labor market remains tight, which could start pushing wages up if energy shocks ease and demand recovers.
moderate: German CPI printed 1.9% in February, well below the 2.2% full-year forecast, signaling that energy-driven inflation fears have not materialized as sharply as feared six months ago.

Domestic consumption is propping up growth despite weak exports, a reversal from Germany's historical reliance on trade surpluses. The 3.6% unemployment rate is lower than the eurozone average of 7.7%, which limits the room for wages to fall and keeps household spending resilient.
The ECB holds rates at 2.15% while the market prices in a move to 2.5% by year-end, but low actual inflation may force the central bank to pause sooner than investors expect.
expert: February CPI of 1.9% sits 30 basis points below full-year guidance and signals supply-side relief is offsetting geopolitical cost pressures; the 3.6% unemployment floor constrains deflationary dynamics.

Domestic demand absorbing external weakness (trade partners sluggish, energy costs elevated) represents a structural shift away from export-led growth. The current account surplus of +4.5% GDP masks weakening external competitiveness that may force policy adjustment.

Watch for Q2 wage negotiations in manufacturing. If unit labor costs accelerate despite low headline CPI, the ECB may be forced to signal a 50 basis point hold at mid-year rather than follow the market's 2.5% terminal rate path.

beginner: France's inflation has collapsed to 0.9%, the lowest among major economies, which means the central bank has very little reason to keep raising interest rates and may even start cutting soon.
Unemployment sits at 7.7%, more than double Germany's rate, revealing a labor market that remains structurally weak despite nearly a decade of recovery since the eurozone crisis.

Rising energy costs from Middle East tensions are hitting French growth projections, but weak domestic demand (reflected in near-zero inflation) means the government has fiscal space to cushion the hit without sparking price pressures.
moderate: French CPI collapsed to 0.9% in February, the lowest reading in the G7, and sits 110 basis points below the 2% full-year forecast. This deflationary lean suggests the economy is running well below potential despite geopolitical headwinds.

The 7.7% unemployment rate is the legacy of rigid labor markets and structural mismatches. Unlike Germany, where tight labor (3.6% unemployment) supports wage growth and demand, France's slack labor market dampens inflation but also caps wage income.
The ECB holds rates at 2.15% but the bond market is pricing in a 35 basis point cut by year-end. The gap between policy and market expectations widens if disinflation accelerates further.
expert: February CPI of 0.9% prints 110 basis points below forecast and signals demand destruction is front-loaded; the 7.7% unemployment rate (eurozone wide) vs. Germany's 3.6% creates a transmission mechanism for deflationary dynamics that will persist even if energy shocks fade.

France's budget deficit is projected at 4.8% of GDP, the weakest major economy ratio after Italy, yet low inflation creates a paradox: the fiscal space exists to stimulate, but political constraints on spending prevent its use.

Watch for ECB forward guidance in May. If the April CPI print (due early May) confirms the sub-1% trend, the central bank will likely abandon its 2.5% terminal rate and signal cuts beginning in June, forcing a 90 basis point policy repricing.

beginner: Italy's inflation at 1.51% is tracking below the 2.3% forecast, which means the country is not facing the price surge some feared from geopolitical shocks, giving the government room to spend without reigniting old inflation demons.
Unemployment at 5.6% is the lowest among Southern Europe but still significantly higher than Germany, reflecting Italy's ongoing structural labor market challenges even as the eurozone recovers.
Italy's large budget deficit of 3.2% reflects elevated spending amid modest growth, a pattern that has limited room to expand further without sparking yields or drawing EU scrutiny.
moderate: Italian CPI printed 1.51% in February, tracking 79 basis points below the 2.3% full-year forecast, which narrows the political risk of EU fiscal rules triggering sanctions on deficit spending.

The 5.6% unemployment rate is the lowest among Southern European peers but remains 2 percentage points above Germany, constraining wage growth and limiting the transmission of tight labor to domestic demand.

Italy's current account surplus of +0.8% GDP and membership in the creditor bloc (Austria, Germany, Netherlands) creates a structural tension: the economy needs fiscal stimulus to raise growth above 1%, but the creditor consensus constrains Berlin and Rome alike.
expert: February CPI of 1.51% vs. 2.3% forecast implies demand-side slack is outpacing energy-cost pass-through; the 5.6% unemployment floor (vs. 3.6% Germany) limits wage spiral risk and gives the ECB cover to hold rates if disinflation spreads to core.

Italy's budget deficit at 3.2% of GDP exceeds the 2.9% EU medium-term objective but remains below France (4.8%) and within the European Commission's informal tolerance band if growth accelerates above 1.5%.

Monitor Q2 wage data. If unit labor costs remain flat despite 1.5% CPI, the ECB will have political cover to shift from 2.5% terminal rate to a 2.0% hold, forcing a repricing of Italian spreads vs. Germany (currently at 120 basis points).

beginner: China's growth forecast just got bumped up to 4.4% this year as the government opens the fiscal taps to support the economy, but the real story is that growth is still slowing from 5.0% last year, signaling Beijing is running out of easy fixes.

Inflation collapsed to just 0.23% in January, the lowest print in years, which means the Chinese economy has massive spare capacity and the government's stimulus is going into restocking warehouses, not driving prices up.
Beijing is pushing hard with fiscal support while the central bank holds rates steady, a sign they are betting on spending growth rather than cheap money to reignite demand.
moderate: China's growth forecast was revised up 20 basis points to 4.4% on the assumption of expanded fiscal stimulus, yet the underlying 2026 forecast of 4.6% (down from 5.0% in 2025) reveals the slowdown is structural, not cyclical. Fiscal tightening cannot reverse demographic and debt headwinds.

CPI of 0.23% in January is disinflation running at full throttle, with near-zero pass-through from stimulus spending. The slack in the economy is so large that incremental demand fills inventory gaps rather than bidding up prices.

The policy rate holds at or near neutral while the government deploys fiscal, reversing the typical playbook and signaling confidence that the demand response to spending will outpace any need for monetary support. Watch for the Q1 GDP print (mid-April) to confirm the growth path is tracking the upward revision.
expert: Growth forecast upgraded 20 basis points to 4.4%, yet the full-year consensus (4.7%) sits 30 basis points above the central bank's implicit 4.5% comfort zone. Deloitte's 4.5% forecast assumes fiscal multiplier of 1.1+, a heroic assumption given Chinese fiscal leakage and off-balance-sheet constraints.

January CPI of 0.23% is the lowest since 2020 and implies the output gap is 2.5%+ of GDP. The lack of price pass-through into core services (medical, education) signals demand destruction in non-discretionary sectors, not just goods deflation.

Watch for March trade data and April credit impulse prints. If import growth remains below 3% year-over-year and social financing growth decelerates below 8%, the fiscal multiplier is failing and the central bank will be forced to cut policy rates by 50 basis points in May, triggering a yuan devaluation cycle.

beginner: India's economy is accelerating despite global turbulence. The government cut interest rates, and companies can now borrow more cheaply to invest and hire.
Foreign trade deals, especially with Europe, are opening new markets for Indian exports. Combined with lower US tariffs, this keeps growth momentum alive.
Inflation has cooled to 1.33%, giving the central bank room to keep cutting rates without triggering price spirals. That supports spending and investment.
moderate: India's policy rate at 5.25% sits well below the full-year forecast of 6%, signaling aggressive easing even as growth forecasts imply 6.9% this year. The central bank is betting domestic demand can sustain momentum without inflation reigniting.
December CPI of 1.33% sits far below the forecast 4.2% for the full year, suggesting either deflation risks or a sharp second-half rebound. Either way, rate cuts remain politically safe for now.

The 6.9% growth forecast for FY2026 outpaces most emerging markets partly because India is benefiting from lower US tariffs and EU trade agreements while global demand elsewhere stalls. Unemployment at 4.22% remains stable, underpinning consumer confidence.
expert: Policy rate at 5.25% versus 6% forecast implies 75 basis points of cumulative cuts already delivered or signaled. CPI at 1.33% sits 290 basis points below consensus, creating room for further easing without breaching inflation targets.

FY2026 growth at 6.9% tracks ahead of consensus 6.3% as domestic demand absorbs lower financing costs faster than external headwinds (current account deficit at 1.2% of GDP) can offset. Trade agreements with EU and lower US tariffs accelerate this margin.

Watch whether Q1 FY2027 inflation data validates the consensus 4.2% forecast or remains subdued. If deflation persists, the central bank faces a dilemma: cuts support growth but risk currency weakness as carry trades unwind.

beginner: South Africa's central bank held interest rates flat in March, worried about dangers ahead. The governor explicitly warned of elevated risks, signaling no relief for borrowers yet.

Unemployment in South Africa sits at a crushing 31.88%, nearly one in three workers without jobs. This structural crisis persists despite rate holds, suggesting monetary policy alone cannot fix the problem.

Inflation across sub-Saharan Africa is climbing due to oil prices and fertilizer costs squeezing farmers and manufacturers. South Africa sits on the edge of that squeeze, with February CPI at 2.96% still contained but vulnerable to external shocks.
moderate: The SARB's March hold contradicts the full-year forecast of 6.25%, implying rates stay elevated longer than consensus expected. Kganyago's cautious language reflects fears that external commodity shocks (oil, fertilizer) could reignite inflation faster than the bank can respond.

Sub-Saharan Africa median inflation is rising from 3.4% in 2025 to 5% in 2026 due to energy and commodity prices, yet South Africa's February CPI at 2.96% sits well below both its own forecast (3.5%) and regional trajectory. This lag may reflect domestic demand weakness offsetting external price pressures.

Unemployment at 31.88% is a structural trap: it prevents the central bank from easing even if inflation moderates, because jobless demand cannot generate the employment multipliers from rate cuts. The forecast 1.5% growth cannot absorb this cohort.
expert: Policy rate held at 6.75% in February versus forecast 6.25%, with March guidance signaling continued caution. The hold suggests the SARB sees downside inflation risks from demand weakness offsetting upside from commodity prices, keeping rates on hold through at least Q2.

February CPI at 2.96% versus forecast 3.5% and sub-Saharan median rising to 5% indicates South Africa's demand weakness is suppressing headline inflation despite external commodity shocks. This creates a policy trap: easing risks currency depreciation and import-price pass-through, but holding risks deepening unemployment at 31.88%.

Forward signal: if March or April CPI drifts toward 3.5% forecast, the SARB likely cuts 25 basis points in May. If it stays below 3%, the bank holds through mid-year, betting that demand remains too weak to sustain inflation despite external pressures.

beginner: Brazil's central bank cut interest rates in March, bringing them down from the punishing 15% level. The country is taking advantage of higher oil prices to ease pressure on borrowers.
As an oil exporter, Brazil makes money when energy prices spike. This windfall is cushioning the economy from the global slowdown, allowing growth to tick up to 1.9% instead of stalling.

Inflation at 3.81% is still rising, but the central bank is cutting anyway because the government needs cheaper borrowing costs to manage debt. This bet works only if oil stays high and inflation doesn't spike further.
moderate: Brazil's central bank cut rates in March despite inflation at 3.81% (forecast 4.2%), signaling confidence that energy export revenues will stabilize prices. The 15% rate in February versus forecast 12% shows the bank had over-tightened and now unwinds aggressively.

The IMF upgraded Brazil's 2026 growth to 1.9% from prior expectations, mainly because oil export revenues shield the economy from external demand collapse. This is a geopolitical windfall tied to Middle East conflict, not domestic reform.

The forecast warns of tightening financial conditions and inflation reacceleration in 2027 as oil prices normalize and rate cuts work through the demand side. Unemployment at 5.8% remains low, so demand pressure could reignite inflation.
expert: Policy rate at 15.0% in February versus forecast 12% shows the central bank had front-loaded tightening in 2025. March cuts signal a pivot based on oil export revenues (Brazil is a net energy exporter) offsetting external demand weakness, justifying the IMF's 1.9% upgrade from prior 1.7% consensus.

CPI at 3.81% February versus forecast 4.2% implies current account relief from higher energy prices is suppressing headline inflation despite accommodative cuts. Current account deficit forecast at 2.6% of GDP is manageable with petrodollar inflows.

Watch April or May CPI prints for signs of demand acceleration from rate cuts. If inflation ticks above 4%, the central bank will pause cuts and risk 2027 rebound to 5%+ as oil prices revert and lagged demand effects materialize. Budget deficit at 6.7% of GDP leaves no room for policy error.

beginner: Russia's central bank cut interest rates in March even though inflation at 6.01% is climbing. The bank is confident because oil revenues are flooding in from higher global prices, giving the government cushion to ease.

As a major oil exporter benefiting from Middle East tensions, Russia's economy is getting a financial boost while most countries slow down. This windfall funds rate cuts that other central banks cannot afford.
Unemployment is near zero at 2.15%, showing the labor market is tight. Rate cuts will add demand pressure, but oil money gives the central bank room to take that risk.
moderate: Russia's central bank cut rates in March despite January CPI at 6.01% (forecast 4.7%), a divergence explained entirely by petrodollar windfalls offsetting external isolation. The bank is betting elevated oil revenues persist through 2026, justifying easing even as inflation lags nominal cuts.

Russia sits among 12 major oil exporters benefiting from the energy price spike tied to Middle East conflict. Unlike most emerging markets, the central bank cut in March while headline inflation exceeds forecast, implicitly assuming energy export revenues stabilize the ruble and domestic price level.

Policy rate at 15.5% in February versus forecast 12.5% shows the bank had tightened aggressively in 2025, likely to defend the ruble against sanctions-driven capital outflows. March cuts signal confidence that geopolitical petrodollars now stabilize currency and allow demand-side accommodation.
expert: Policy rate at 15.5% February versus forecast 12.5%, with cuts underway in March, indicates the central bank has shifted from defensive tightening (2025) to petrodollar-confident easing. January CPI at 6.01% versus forecast 4.7% reflects lagged pass-through from ruble weakness, not demand overheating.

Current account surplus forecast at 2% of GDP versus 2.6% for Brazil deficit underscores Russia's energy export windfall. Oil revenues stabilize the ruble and allow rate cuts despite inflation running above target, a policy luxury unavailable to non-commodity exporters.

Forward watch: if Brent crude stays above $80, the central bank can sustain cuts through mid-2026 and hit 12.5% forecast by Q3. If oil reverts below $70, inflation likely re-accelerates as ruble weakens and imports reprice, forcing the bank to pause cuts by Q4 2026.

Energy costs are pushing up prices for everything from gas to food across the world

beginner.label: Markets Split on War Response

Asian markets fell sharply as oil prices jumped, showing the global economic strain
Currency markets are favoring the dollar as investors seek safety during the conflict

beginner.label: Federal Reserve Stays Cautious

Officials worry that cutting rates now could make rising prices even worse
The central bank is caught between helping growth and controlling inflation from the oil shock

European markets face deeper pressure as gas storage sits at just 30% capacity after harsh winter conditions

Regional divergence widening: US tech momentum versus EM vulnerability, with IMF cutting global growth to 3.1% in 2026 from 3.2% previously
Corporate credit spreads rising 50-100bp across regions as energy-intensive industrials face margin compression from input cost inflation
